explain:
A P1 incident struck mobile banking, fund transfers and ATMs.
Transfers worth EUR 500,000 queued while customers waited.
The war room restored service in about 40 minutes.
The cause was still unknown.

Here is what happened:

→ P1 declared across mobile banking, fund transfers and ATMs
→ War room restores service in about 40 minutes
→ Customers told service is back
→ A batch process had consumed critical database resources during peak hours
→ The same batch is still scheduled for tomorrow

The requirement said:
"Close the incident once service is restored."

So the incident closed, and the cause that broke it was left running.

Why?

Incident and problem management are two disciplines with different clocks. Incident restores service fast. Problem finds why it happened so it never recurs. Restoring service without fixing the batch overlap only buys 24 hours until the next peak.

Restored is not resolved.

BA Takeaway

Restore and resolve are two different jobs, so keep them separate:

→ Incident timeline, restore the service
→ Problem timeline, find the cause
→ Permanent fix, reschedule the batch and add guards and alerts

The real requirement is not "When was service back?"

It is "What evidence proves the cause is fixed and cannot recur at the next peak?"

Have you ever seen an incident closed as fixed, only for the same cause to strike again the next day?
takeaway: Restored is not resolved.

title: Payments fail only at 11 AM, EUR 90,000 queue stuck
explain:
Every day at 11 AM, payments start timing out.
A queue of EUR 90,000 in payments stalls.
By noon everything works again.
The team keeps fixing the code. The code is fine.

Here is how that happens:

→ Timeouts appear only at peak hours
→ Slow processing, then lagging database queries
→ High server load at peak traffic
→ Servers not sized for peak traffic

The assumption was:
"A failure is a code bug, so fix the code."

Failures that appear only at peak hours point at capacity, not code.

Why?

The 5-Why chain runs from timeouts to slow processing to lagging database queries to high server load to servers not sized for peak traffic. Fixing code leaves the root untouched, so the same timeouts return at the same hour the next day.

Peak-only failures mean capacity.

Why do the same payments fail at 11 AM and pass at noon?

BA Takeaway

Fix the root, then monitor to confirm the failures actually stopped.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Symptom, when the failures happen
→ Root cause, capacity or code, proved by the pattern
→ Fix, indexing, more capacity, load balancing
→ Proof, monitoring that shows the failures stopped

Log the hour of every failure, and treat a peak-only pattern as a capacity case from the start.

The real requirement is not "What code failed?"

It is "What evidence proves the failures stopped at peak, not just moved?"

Have you chased a code bug that turned out to be capacity?
takeaway: Peak-only failures mean capacity. All-day failures mean code or data.

title: USD 2,000,000 trade, no rule says which instrument comes first
explain:
A buyer and seller agree a USD 2,000,000 trade.
The buyer asks which instrument starts it, letter of credit or bank guarantee.
There is no rule that answers that.
The team waits for a rule that does not exist.

Here is how that happens:

→ Trade agreed for USD 2,000,000
→ Buyer asks for the first instrument
→ Team searches the rulebook for a fixed order
→ No rule fixes which instrument a trade starts with

The assumption was:
"The rules pick the first instrument."

No rule fixes which instrument a trade starts with, whether a letter of credit or a bank guarantee.

Why?

The choice depends on many factors, above all how much security both parties want. Greater appetite for security on both sides calls for more sophisticated payment techniques, so the answer is a judgement about the parties, not a lookup in a rulebook.

Security appetite picks the instrument, not a rule.

Why does the team wait for a rule that cannot answer the question?

BA Takeaway

Decide the instrument from the parties' security needs, and record the judgement, not a rule reference.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Letter of credit, one instrument option
→ Bank guarantee, another instrument option
→ Security appetite, what both parties want above all
→ Other factors, the many facts that shape the choice

Write the choice down with the security judgement behind it, so the next trade starts from the reasoning.

The real requirement is not "Which rule picks the instrument?"

It is "What evidence proves the instrument matches the security both parties want?"

Have you waited on a rule that never existed?
takeaway: Greater appetite for security on both sides calls for more sophisticated payment techniques.

title: EUR 600,000 GPP payment, the mapping that nobody tested
explain:
A EUR 600,000 payment goes through GPP.
The ISO 20022 mapping was never tested with this message type.
The payment fails at mapping, is routed wrong, and posts twice.
Three failures, one untested stage.

Here is how that happens:

→ ISO 20022 mapping, mapping can fail or delay the payment
→ Routing, wrong route delays or fails the payment
→ Duplicate handling, duplicates must be caught before posting
→ Core banking integration, integration gaps stall the payment
→ Testing and reconciliation, each stage needs its own proof

The assumption was:
"Test the flow end to end and every stage is covered."

The GPP end-to-end flow has real implementation challenges: ISO 20022 mapping, routing, duplicates, core banking integration, testing and reconciliation.

Why?

Each of these is a place where a payment can fail or be delayed, and each needs its own design and test coverage. An end-to-end test that passes on the happy path proves nothing about the mapping of a new message type or the duplicate check under a retry.

A happy path test is not stage coverage.

Why does a tested flow fail at mapping, routing and posting at once?

BA Takeaway

Give each challenge its own design and its own test coverage, and prove each stage separately.

Keep these controls separate:

→ ISO 20022 mapping, tested per message type
→ Routing, tested per route
→ Duplicates, caught before posting
→ Core banking integration, tested per posting
→ Reconciliation, proving the payment completed correctly

Show test coverage per stage, not just one end-to-end pass.

The real requirement is not "Did the flow pass testing?"

It is "What evidence proves each stage was designed and tested on its own?"

Have you seen a happy path test hide three stage failures?
takeaway: Each of these is a place where a payment can fail or be delayed, and each needs its own design and test coverage.

title: EUR 200,000 API change, the endpoint looked simple, the blast radius was not
explain:
A team changes an API endpoint for a EUR 200,000 payment flow.
The endpoint looks simple, one field added.
Three downstream systems break.
Nobody mapped the consumers.

Here is how that happens:

→ Endpoint changed, one field added
→ Data, consumers and dependencies never mapped
→ Downstream systems read the changed payload
→ Three break, each in a different way

The assumption was:
"The endpoint is the API."

Analysing an API means looking beyond the endpoint.

Why?

A BA must understand the data, the consumers, the dependencies and the impact of a change, because an API that looks simple at the endpoint can have deep downstream effects. The endpoint is only the surface, and the blast radius lives underneath it.

The endpoint is only the surface.

Why does one added field break three systems?

BA Takeaway

Map data, consumers, dependencies and impact before any API change ships.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Data, what the API carries and changes
→ Consumers, who calls the API
→ Dependencies, what the API relies on downstream
→ Impact of change, what a change breaks or moves
→ The endpoint, only the surface, not the whole API

List every consumer and dependency on the change record, and confirm each one before release.

The real requirement is not "Did the endpoint change?"

It is "What evidence proves every consumer and dependency still works after the change?"

Have you seen a small endpoint change break systems nobody mapped?
takeaway: A BA must understand the data, the consumers, the dependencies and the impact of a change.

title: EUR 350,000 requirement written without API knowledge, misses the payload gap
explain:
A BA writes a requirement for a EUR 350,000 payment flow.
The requirement looks complete.
Development finds a payload gap on day one.
The BA could not see it, because the API was never understood.

Here is how that happens:

→ Requirement written from the business view only
→ Endpoints, payloads and data gaps never examined
→ Impact, security and backward compatibility never assessed
→ Development stalls on a gap the requirement never named

The assumption was:
"Business requirements do not need API knowledge."

A BA who understands APIs can work with endpoints, payloads, data gaps, impact analysis, security and backward compatibility.

Why?

Without that knowledge, the BA cannot write a complete requirement or assess the impact of a change. The gap is not a development surprise, it is a requirement that was written blind to the API it describes.

A requirement without API knowledge is incomplete by definition.

Why does a complete-looking requirement stall development on day one?

BA Takeaway

Learn the API before writing the requirement, and name the payload, the gaps and the compatibility in it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Endpoints, where the API is called
→ Payloads, what the API carries
→ Data gaps, what is missing in the data
→ Impact analysis, what a change affects
→ Security and backward compatibility, old callers keep working

Attach the endpoint and payload to every API requirement, with the data gaps listed.

The real requirement is not "Is the business need clear?"

It is "What evidence proves the requirement covers the API it describes?"

Have you written a requirement that stalled on a payload gap?
takeaway: Without API knowledge, the BA cannot write a complete requirement or assess the impact of a change.

title: The vendor feature that worked everywhere except where it mattered
explain:
A vendor demos a capability the bank needs.

It works beautifully on screen. It only works globally.

The bank needs it per country. The feature is useless.

Here is how it happens:

→ Vendor demos the capability
→ The bank signs up
→ Configuration only works at global level
→ The country rule cannot be set
→ The capability cannot be used where it matters

The requirement said:
"The vendor says the capability exists."

Why?

A capability that only works globally, when the bank needs it per country, by entity, by product or by payment type, is not fit for purpose. A demoed feature and a usable feature are not the same thing.

A demoed feature is not a usable feature.

BA Takeaway

Verify the configuration granularity before accepting that a requirement is met. Ask at which level it can be configured, and prove it with a test, not a demo.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The capability itself
→ The level it can be configured at
→ The acceptance test that proves it

The real requirement is not "Does the capability exist?"

It is "What evidence proves the capability works at the level the business needs?"

Have you accepted a vendor feature on a demo, only to find it could not be configured where it mattered?
takeaway: A demoed feature is not a usable feature. Verify the configuration level first.

title: The EUR 45,000 payment that failed in the place nobody planned for
explain:
A EUR 45,000 payment is processed with the wrong details, and the verification of payee check fails.

The team has no alternative ready, and no communication plan.

The customer finds out from the beneficiary, not from the bank.

Here is how it happens:

→ Solution goes live
→ Requirements change, and the change was captured wrongly
→ Processing is delayed, and a system slows down
→ Payment is processed with wrong details
→ No alternative is ready, and no one tells the customer

The assumption was:
"The solution will work."

Why?

A payment solution can fail in three places: functionally, when requirements change or were captured wrongly; technically, when processing is delayed, a system is down or performance drops; and in business terms, when a payment is processed with wrong details or a check like verification of payee fails.

Design for failure, or failure designs the day.

BA Takeaway

Plan for each kind of failure, know the alternative when a solution fails, and keep a communication plan with the business and stakeholders. One payment change rarely touches only one application.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Functional failure plan
→ Technical failure plan
→ Business failure plan

The real requirement is not "Will the solution work?"

It is "What evidence proves we know the alternative when this solution fails?"

Have you seen a payment fail in the one place nobody planned for?
takeaway: Design for failure, or failure designs the day. Plan for all three places a solution can fail.

title: Schedule it for next week: the five rules hidden in one sentence
explain:
A customer asks to schedule a EUR 25,000 payment for next week.

It sounds simple. It hides five rules.

The system accepts a past date, cannot reschedule it, and nobody knows what happens when the date passes unprocessed.

Here is how it happens:

→ Customer asks to schedule a payment
→ Requirement is written down as one sentence
→ No rule stops a past date
→ No rule covers rescheduling with a new effective date
→ No rule cancels it when it is not processed on the requested date
→ In a request to pay such as pain.013, the execution date shows even when the data is empty

The assumption was:
"Document what the customer asked."

Why?

A high-level need has to be decoded into business rules: a payment can be set for a future date, recreated or rescheduled with a new effective date, never scheduled for a date in the past, scheduled for several payment types, and cancelled when it is not processed on the requested date.

A requirement that cannot be written as a rule is not a simple requirement.

BA Takeaway

Find the business rule behind the requirement rather than mapping one field to another.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Future date rule
→ Reschedule rule
→ Cancel rule

The real requirement is not "What did the customer ask for?"

It is "What evidence proves the rule behind the requirement is written down?"

Have you seen a one-sentence requirement hide five rules?
takeaway: A requirement that cannot be written as a rule is not a simple requirement. Decode it, do not just document it.

title: The customers failing five times a day that nobody noticed
explain:
Customers are failing payments five times a day, every day.

Nobody notices, because the rule to find them was never defined.

By the time the complaints arrive, the customers have already left.

Here is how it happens:

→ No time window is defined
→ No failure condition is defined
→ No threshold is set for what counts as repeated
→ Test transactions and duplicates are counted as real failures
→ The wrong customers are targeted, and the real ones are missed

The assumption was:
"Count the failures."

Why?

Finding customers with repeated failed transactions means translating the business rule into a time-windowed aggregation: define the window, the failure condition and the threshold, then aggregate and validate the data quality before acting. A count that includes test transactions, duplicates or a wrong window will target the wrong customers.

A precise rule plus clean data is the whole method.

BA Takeaway

Define the window, the condition and the threshold first, then check the data quality before acting on the result.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Time window
→ Failure condition and threshold
→ Data quality check

The real requirement is not "How many failures?"

It is "What evidence proves the count excludes tests and duplicates?"

Have you seen a team act on a failure count that included test transactions?
takeaway: A precise rule plus clean data is the whole method.

title: The EUR 75,000 payment rule nobody could test
explain:
A business asks for a rule on EUR 75,000 payments.

The requirement is written down as one vague sentence.

It is built, and the problem is found in testing, when fixing it costs ten times more.

Here is how it happens:

→ Requirement arrives vague and ambiguous
→ It is written down without discovery questions
→ No concrete examples pin down the behaviour
→ No one observes how the work is really done
→ No playback confirms the understanding
→ Testing finds the misunderstanding

The assumption was:
"Write down what the business said."

Why?

Ambiguity is normal at the start of a requirement. Discovery questions find what is actually meant, concrete examples pin down the behaviour, process observation shows how the work is really done, and playback confirms the understanding with stakeholders.

Ambiguity handled early is cheap; ambiguity found in testing is expensive.

BA Takeaway

The output must be a requirement that is testable: an observable outcome, a boundary condition and an acceptance criterion, rather than a vague wish no one can verify.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Discovery questions
→ Concrete examples and observation
→ Playback with stakeholders

The real requirement is not "What did the business say?"

It is "What evidence proves the requirement states an observable outcome?"

Have you seen a vague requirement found in testing, when it was already expensive to fix?
takeaway: Ambiguity handled early is cheap; ambiguity found in testing is expensive.

title: The requirement that passed review and failed every test
explain:
A requirement for a EUR 60,000 payment flow passes review.

It fails every test, because no test can prove it.

The team argues about whether it was delivered, and there is no way to resolve the dispute.

Here is how it happens:

→ Observable outcome is stated
→ Boundary conditions are missing
→ Negative cases are missing
→ Acceptance criteria are missing
→ No one can verify the requirement
→ Delivery is disputed

The assumption was:
"The requirement is written, so it is testable."

Why?

A requirement is testable when it defines an observable outcome, the boundary conditions, the negative cases and the acceptance criteria. Without these four, a requirement cannot be verified.

Without these four, a requirement cannot be verified.

BA Takeaway

Check every requirement for all four parts before it leaves analysis. A missing part is a dispute waiting to happen.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Observable outcome
→ Boundary conditions
→ Negative cases
→ Acceptance criteria

The real requirement is not "Is it written down?"

It is "What evidence proves this requirement can pass or fail?"

title: Two stakeholders, one EUR 200,000 decision, no record of why
explain:
Two stakeholders disagree over a EUR 200,000 payment flow decision.

A compromise is reached in the meeting.

Next month the same stakeholders meet, and the same argument reopens, because nobody wrote down the decision.

Here is how it happens:

→ Competing requirements clash
→ Value, risk, urgency, customer impact and dependencies are debated
→ A decision is made
→ The decision, who made it and why, is not documented
→ The compromise is reopened at the next meeting

The assumption was:
"We agreed in the meeting."

Why?

The comparison must be evidence based, so each stakeholder can see why one requirement was chosen over another. An undocumented compromise will be reopened the next time the same stakeholders meet.

Document the decision, who made it and why.

BA Takeaway

Facilitate a documented decision on evidence, and record who made it and why.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Evidence based comparison
→ The decision
→ The record of who decided and why

The real requirement is not "Did we agree?"

It is "What evidence proves the decision and its reason survive the meeting?"

Have you seen the same argument reopen because the decision was never written down?

title: The business asked in plain words, and the system was built in system words
explain:
A non-technical stakeholder describes a EUR 40,000 payment need in business language.

The team builds it in system language.

Playback is skipped, the misunderstanding is found after the build, and the rework costs a sprint.

Here is how it happens:

→ Interviews hear the need in business language
→ Workshops build shared understanding
→ Observation shows how the work is actually done
→ Examples pin down the detail
→ Structured playback is skipped
→ The build reflects the misunderstanding

The assumption was:
"We heard the requirement."

Why?

Non-technical stakeholders describe what they need in business language, not in system language. Playback matters most, because it catches misunderstandings while they are still cheap to fix.

Confirm before you write, not after you build.

BA Takeaway

Run structured playback before the requirement is written down, and let the stakeholder recognise their own need in it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Interviews and workshops
→ Observation and examples
→ Structured playback

The real requirement is not "Did we hear them?"

It is "What evidence proves the stakeholder recognised their own need in the playback?"

title: The missing rule found in UAT, and the EUR 60,000 fix that followed
explain:
A missing rule is found in UAT.

The fix costs EUR 60,000, because the gap was lost in discovery and a whole stage must be reworked.

The team fixes the symptom. The same gap recurs next release.

Here is how it happens:

→ A piece of the need is missed
→ The gap is found late, in UAT
→ The fix is applied to the symptom
→ The origin is never traced
→ The same gap recurs

The assumption was:
"Fix the symptom."

Why?

Tracing the gap to its origin matters because it decides whether the fix is a small correction or a rework of a whole stage, and it prevents the same gap from recurring. The gap could have been lost in discovery, analysis, design, implementation or testing.

Fix the origin, not just the symptom.

BA Takeaway

Trace the gap back to where it was lost, and agree corrective action with the owner of that stage.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Discovery and analysis
→ Design and implementation
→ Testing

The real requirement is not "What is the fix?"

It is "What evidence proves where the gap was lost?"

Have you seen the same gap recur because the origin was never traced?
takeaway: Fix the origin, not just the symptom.

title: The process diagram that misled everyone who used it
explain:
A process diagram for a EUR 100,000 payment flow is drawn from assumptions.

It looks right. It is wrong.

The team follows it, and every hand-off goes to the wrong place.

Here is how it happens:

→ Diagram is drawn
→ Actors, triggers, decisions, hand-offs and data stores are assumed
→ Nothing is checked against reality
→ Diagram is never validated with the people who do the work
→ Everyone who relies on it is misled

The assumption was:
"The diagram looks right."

Why?

A process diagram must show the actors, the triggers, the decisions, the hand-offs and the data stores, and each of these must be checked against reality rather than assumed.

A diagram is only as good as its validation.

BA Takeaway

Validate the diagram with the people who do the work. Choose the diagram that fits the problem, then prove it matches reality.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Actors and triggers
→ Decisions and hand-offs
→ Data stores and validation

The real requirement is not "Is the diagram drawn?"

It is "What evidence proves the diagram matches the real process?"

title: The requirements signed off in a day, and rebuilt over six weeks
explain:
Requirements for a EUR 80,000 payment change are signed off in a day.

Validation is skipped to save time.

The rebuild takes six weeks, because the misunderstandings were found in development and testing instead.

Here is how it happens:

→ Walkthroughs are skipped
→ Consistency checks are skipped
→ Testability checks are skipped
→ Sign-off is given
→ Misunderstandings surface in development and testing
→ Fixes cost far more than validation would have

The assumption was:
"Sign-off means the requirements are ready."

Why?

A walkthrough catches misunderstandings, a consistency check catches contradictions, a testability check catches requirements that cannot be verified, and sign-off records agreement. Skipping validation does not save time; it moves the cost into development and testing.

Skipping validation does not save time; it moves the cost.

BA Takeaway

Run walkthroughs, consistency checks, testability checks and formal sign-off before development starts.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Walkthroughs
→ Consistency checks
→ Testability checks
→ Formal sign-off

The real requirement is not "Are they signed off?"

It is "What evidence proves the requirement set was validated before development?"

title: The change nobody could trace, and the release it broke
explain:
A change is made to a EUR 120,000 payment flow.

Nobody can trace it forward to its impact.

The release breaks, and nobody can trace the defect back to its origin.

Here is how it happens:

→ Business objective is set
→ Requirement is written
→ Story and design follow
→ Tests are run
→ A defect appears
→ No chain links the defect back to its origin

The assumption was:
"We know what changed."

Why?

A traceability matrix connects business objectives to requirements, stories, design, tests, defects and release evidence, with each row showing the chain from the objective through the requirement to the test that proves it. Any change can then be traced forward to its impact and any defect traced back to its origin.

Without traceability, a team cannot prove what was built is what was asked for.

BA Takeaway

Keep the chain intact from objective to release evidence, or a change cannot be assessed safely.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Objectives and requirements
→ Stories and design
→ Tests, defects and release evidence

The real requirement is not "What changed?"

It is "What evidence proves this change traces forward to its impact?"

Have you seen a release break because nobody could trace a change to its impact?
takeaway: Without traceability, a team cannot prove that what was built is what was asked for, and cannot assess the impact of a change safely.

title: The scope that shrank one change at a time
explain:
Requirements for a EUR 150,000 payment project change every week.

Each change is small. The delivery date slips, and nobody can say why.

The scope eroded one uncosted change at a time.

Here is how it happens:

→ Change is requested
→ No change intake records what is asked and why
→ No impact analysis states the cost in scope, effort and risk
→ No prioritisation ranks it against other work
→ No decision governance records who approved it
→ Weekly changes silently erode the scope and the delivery date

The assumption was:
"It is only a small change."

Why?

Change intake, impact analysis, prioritisation and decision governance are the discipline that keeps weekly change visible. Without them, the erosion is silent.

Without this discipline, weekly changes silently erode the scope and the delivery date.

BA Takeaway

Record every change, cost it, rank it and record who approved it, or the date will move without anyone deciding it should.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Change intake
→ Impact analysis
→ Prioritisation
→ Decision governance

The real requirement is not "Is the change small?"

It is "What evidence proves each change was costed before it was accepted?"

Have you seen a delivery date slip one small change at a time?
takeaway: Without this discipline, weekly changes silently erode the scope and the delivery date.

title: Two weeks wanted, six estimated, and the EUR 150,000 decision in between
explain:
The business wants a EUR 150,000 payment feature in two weeks.

Development estimates six.

The meeting argues over the number, and nobody decides what to deliver.

Here is how it happens:

→ Business wants two weeks, development estimates six
→ The minimum outcome that would still be valuable is never clarified
→ Scope is never sliced to the smallest useful increment
→ Dependencies that drive the estimate are never identified
→ Trade-offs are argued, not evidenced

The assumption was:
"Argue the estimate."

Why?

Clarify the minimum outcome, slice the scope, identify the dependencies, and present evidence based trade-offs. The decision is then about what to deliver and what to defer, not about whose estimate is right.

The decision is about what to deliver and what to defer.

BA Takeaway

Turn an estimate argument into a scope decision, with evidence in front of the people who must choose.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Minimum valuable outcome
→ Sliced scope
→ Dependencies
→ Evidence based trade-offs

The real requirement is not "Whose estimate is right?"

It is "What evidence proves the smallest useful increment is agreed?"

Have you seen a two-week versus six-week argument settled by slicing the scope instead?
takeaway: The decision is then about what to deliver and what to defer, not about whose estimate is right.

title: Build us the solution, said the board, and nobody asked what problem it solved
explain:
Senior management asks for a solution for a EUR 200,000 payment problem.

No requirements are given. The team builds the solution anyway.

It does not solve the real problem, because nobody asked what the problem was.

Here is how it happens:

→ Solution is requested without requirements
→ No one asks what outcome is needed
→ No one asks what constraints apply
→ No one asks what options exist
→ No one asks what criteria will decide between them
→ The wrong solution is built on time

The assumption was:
"Build the solution they asked for."

Why?

Reframing the request around outcomes, constraints, options and decision criteria turns a request for a specific solution into a decision that can be made on evidence, and avoids building something that does not solve the real problem.

Reframe the ask before you build the answer.

BA Takeaway

Ask what outcome is needed, what constraints apply, what options exist and what criteria will decide, before any build starts.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Outcomes
→ Constraints
→ Options and decision criteria

The real requirement is not "What solution was asked for?"

It is "What evidence proves we know the outcome before we choose the solution?"

Have you built a solution that answered the ask and missed the problem?
takeaway: Reframe the ask before you build the answer.

title: Complete, said the business. Incomplete, said the developers.
explain:
The business believes the requirements for a EUR 90,000 payment change are complete.

The developers disagree.

Both sides read the same words and understand different things, and the rebuild starts before anyone notices.

Here is how it happens:

→ Requirements are declared complete
→ Developers read them differently
→ Concrete examples are never used to show how each side reads them
→ No walkthrough surfaces the differences
→ Traceability never shows what is covered and what is not
→ Shared definitions are never agreed

The assumption was:
"The requirements are complete."

Why?

The gap is usually in interpretation rather than in content. Close the interpretation gap before development, because it is far cheaper to agree on meaning now than to rebuild later.

Close the interpretation gap before development.

BA Takeaway

Use concrete examples, walkthroughs, traceability and shared definitions to prove both sides read the requirement the same way.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Concrete examples
→ Walkthroughs
→ Traceability and shared definitions

The real requirement is not "Are the requirements complete?"

It is "What evidence proves both sides read the requirement the same way?"

Have you seen a build start while two sides read the same requirement differently?
takeaway: Close the interpretation gap before development, because it is far cheaper to agree on meaning now than to rebuild later.

title: The new payment screen nobody used
explain:
A new digital payment screen is launched.

Nobody uses it.

The team calls the users stubborn. The resistance has a cause nobody bothered to find.

Here is how it happens:

→ Digital change is launched
→ Impacts on each user group are never mapped
→ Stakeholder concerns are never identified
→ Training needs are never defined
→ No champions support the change
→ Feedback is never collected, and adoption is never measured

The assumption was:
"Users are just stubborn."

Why?

User resistance to a digital change usually has a cause that can be identified. Resistance that is understood can be addressed; resistance that is dismissed as stubbornness will grow and will damage the change.

Diagnose resistance before you try to overcome it.

BA Takeaway

Map the impacts, identify the concerns, define the training, find champions, collect feedback and measure adoption.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Impacts and concerns
→ Training needs
→ Champions, feedback and adoption

The real requirement is not "How do we push users to adopt it?"

It is "What evidence proves we understand why users resist?"

Have you seen a launch fail because resistance was dismissed instead of diagnosed?
takeaway: Diagnose resistance before you try to overcome it.

title: The BA who could not prove the EUR 300,000 saving
explain:
A process change claims a EUR 300,000 saving.

Stakeholders ask for the proof.

There is none. Nothing was measured before, and nothing was measured after.

Here is how it happens:

→ Process change is delivered
→ Cost is never measured before and after
→ Cycle time is never measured
→ Error rates are never measured
→ Customer experience is never measured
→ Benefits realisation is never done

The assumption was:
"The improvement is obvious."

Why?

An analyst demonstrates contribution by connecting process changes to measurable outcomes: link the change to cost, cycle time, error rates, customer experience and benefits realisation, and measure before and after so the improvement can be shown rather than claimed.

Measured value is the analyst's evidence, not a claim.

BA Takeaway

Measure before and after, and finish with benefits realisation, because it proves the change delivered the value that justified it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Cost and cycle time
→ Error rates and customer experience
→ Benefits realisation

The real requirement is not "Did we deliver the change?"

It is "What evidence proves the change delivered the value that justified it?"

Have you seen a claimed saving dismissed because nobody measured it?
takeaway: Measured value is the analyst's evidence, not a claim.

title: The mid-sprint change that broke the sprint goal
explain:
A change is requested mid-sprint on a EUR 100,000 payment feature.

It is accepted on the spot, without assessment.

The sprint goal breaks, and the team is held accountable for a target it never agreed to.

Here is how it happens:

→ Change is requested mid-sprint
→ Scope is never assessed
→ Impact on the sprint goal is never assessed
→ Effort is never assessed
→ Dependencies are never assessed
→ Change is accepted, and the goal silently breaks

The assumption was:
"Just fit it in."

Why?

A change requested mid-sprint must be assessed before it is agreed: scope, impact on the sprint goal, effort required and dependencies introduced. Only then decide whether to accept it, defer it or swap it for something else.

Accepting a change without assessment silently breaks the sprint goal.

BA Takeaway

Assess first, decide second. Accept, defer or swap only with the evidence in front of the team.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Scope of the change
→ Impact on the sprint goal
→ Effort and dependencies

The real requirement is not "Can we fit it in?"

It is "What evidence proves the sprint goal survives this change?"

title: The change that arrived when 70 percent of the sprint was done
explain:
A change is requested when 70 percent of the sprint is done.

The team absorbs it quietly to be helpful.

The sprint goal is compromised, and nobody decided that it should be.

Here is how it happens:

→ Change arrives late in the sprint
→ Reason for the change is never established
→ Effort is never assessed
→ Dependencies are never assessed
→ Options are never laid out for the product owner
→ Team absorbs the change and the goal slips

The assumption was:
"The team can absorb it."

Why?

A late change needs a careful assessment: establish the reason, the effort, the dependencies and the options the product owner has, and do not silently compromise the sprint goal to absorb it. The product owner decides, with the evidence in front of them, whether the change is worth the disruption or whether it waits for the next sprint.

A late change is a decision, not an instruction.

BA Takeaway

Present the options with the evidence, and let the product owner decide. Never let a late change silently void the sprint goal.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Reason for the change
→ Effort and dependencies
→ Options for the product owner

The real requirement is not "Can the team absorb it?"

It is "What evidence proves the product owner chose with the full cost in front of them?"

Have you seen a late change absorbed quietly, and the sprint goal pay for it?
takeaway: A late change is a decision, not an instruction.

title: Two senior stakeholders, opposite outcomes, one undocumented call
explain:
Two senior stakeholders want opposite outcomes on a EUR 250,000 payment decision.

A call is made in the room.

It is never documented, and the debate reopens at the next meeting.

Here is how it happens:

→ Two senior stakeholders want opposite outcomes
→ Value, risk, cost and customer impact are debated
→ Evidence drives the ranking
→ A decision is made
→ Who made it and why is never recorded
→ The debate reopens

The assumption was:
"The senior person decides."

Why?

Facilitate an evidence based prioritisation and document the accountable decision. A documented decision ends the debate; an undocumented one will be reopened every time the stakeholders meet.

A documented decision ends the debate.

Lay out the value, the risk, the cost and the customer impact of each requirement, let the evidence drive the ranking, and record who made the decision and why.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Evidence for each option
→ The decision
→ The record of who decided and why

The real requirement is not "Who is senior?"

It is "What evidence proves who decided, and why?"

takeaway: A documented decision ends the debate; an undocumented one will be reopened every time the stakeholders meet.

A change approved without this assessment can invalidate the testing that has already been done and put the release date at risk.

Never let a late change silently void completed testing.

Assess requirement impact, test scope, release risk and decision rights before approving any change this close to UAT.

→ Test scope

→ Decision rights

The real requirement is not "Is the change small?"

It is "What evidence proves completed testing still stands after this change?"
